unit.unitOverview: This unit is about how things are made, grown, sold and mended. You will learn to describe a process without naming the person who does the work: the bags are made here, the cotton is grown on small farms. You will learn one word for a whole group, and the name of a process. By the end you can explain how an everyday object reaches a shop.
unit.learningPath:
Meet 30 words for making, materials, groups and industry.
Read a short visit to a repair shop, an information page and a real product label.
Learn is made, are grown, is sold: when the doer does not matter.
Learn was delivered, were repaired: the same, once it is over.
Pick the group word that fits: a crowd, a flock, a herd.
Turn a verb into the name of its process: deliver, delivery.
Speak and write, and check every answer against the key.
Take the quiz, then record your unit assignment.

visual.lectureScript:
Welcome to Unit 16. This unit is about how things are made.
You will learn to describe a process without naming the person who does the work.
Start with the words for making and growing.
To manufacture is to make something in large numbers, with machines.
To assemble is to put the parts of something together.
To package is to put a thing in a box or a bag before it is sold.
To harvest is to cut and collect a crop when it is ready.
To process is to treat something by machine, step by step, until it is ready to use.
To repair is to fix something that is broken.
Two words are often swapped: export and import.
You export goods out to another country. You import goods in from another country.
Now the materials.
Cotton grows on a plant. Wool is the warm hair of a sheep.
Leather is made from animal skin. Steel is a hard, strong metal.
Clay is heavy earth that goes hard when it is heated.
Rubber bends and keeps water out. Concrete builds walls, floors and bridges.
Fabric is the material your clothes are made of.
Now the group words.
A crowd of people. A flock of birds. A herd of cows.
A bunch of keys. A set of tools. A pile of boxes.
A crew of workers. A collection of old photos.
Each group word goes with particular things. Learn the pair, not the word.
A herd of birds is wrong. Birds go in a flock.
Last, four words for the work itself.
An industry is all the factories and work of one kind, taken together.
A factory is the building. A product is the thing that is made.
A material is what the product is made of.
Waste is what is left over. Profit is the money left after the costs.
Now the first pattern.
Look at the label inside a jacket. It says: made of cotton.
Nobody is named there, and nobody needs to be.
English says this with two pieces.
The first piece is is or are.
The second piece is the past form of the verb.
The bags are made here. The cotton is grown on small farms.
This bread is sold in the market.
The thing you are talking about comes first.
One thing takes is. More than one takes are.
The past form is the same one you use after have. Made, grown, sold, sent.
Say the two pieces together. Is made. Are grown.
If you stop after are, the sentence is not finished.
Now the second pattern.
For something that has already happened, change is to was, and are to were.
The chair was repaired on Friday.
The boxes were delivered at the side gate.
Nothing else moves. Repaired stays repaired.
Ask a question the same way. When was it delivered? Where were they made?
Now the third pattern.
A group word names a whole group in one word.
It is not free. Each one goes with particular things.
People stand in a crowd. Birds fly in a flock. Cows move in a herd.
Keys hang in a bunch. Tools come in a set. Boxes stand in a pile.
Workers on one job are a crew. Photos kept for years are a collection.
And the fourth pattern.
Every verb here has a noun beside it: the name of the process.
Produce, production. Deliver, delivery. Collect, collection.
Assemble, assembly. Pay, payment. Protect, protection.
Some do not change at all. Repair, repair. Waste, waste.
Notices use the noun, because it is shorter.
The delivery is on Friday. Repairs are free for one year.
Now read the three texts.
The first is a short visit to a repair shop.
The second explains how a cotton shirt is made.
The third is a product label and a notice at a factory gate.
Then do the practice, and check every answer against the key.
Record your speaking, and play it back.
At the end, describe one object near you: what it is made of, and how it reaches a shop.

readings.title: The chair with the broken leg
readings.setting: A small repair shop at the end of a street
readings.passageScript:
There is a small repair shop at the end of the street. The door is open from eight in the morning. Inside there is a long bench, a pile of tools and a set of old chairs.

Lena carries in a chair with a broken leg.

Lena: Good morning. Can you repair this chair?
Worker: Let me look. Yes. The leg is broken, but the wood is good.
Lena: It is very old. My grandmother sat in it.
Worker: I can see that. Nothing here is manufactured now. This one was assembled by hand.
Lena: How long does it take?
Worker: The leg is glued today. Then it is left for two days. The whole chair is cleaned on Friday.
Lena: And the price?
Worker: Twenty for the repair. Nothing for the cleaning.
Lena: Do you deliver?
Worker: Deliveries are made on Saturday morning. The crew takes six or seven pieces each week.
Lena: Thank you. A neighbour sent me here.
Worker: We are not the fastest. We are careful. Every piece is checked twice before it leaves.

Lena signs a card at the counter. The card is put on the chair with a number on it. A collection of cards hangs on the wall behind the bench. Each one is a job that is waiting.

The chair is carried to the back of the shop. The door is open again at eight tomorrow.

readings.title: From the field to the shirt
readings.setting: A cotton farm, a mill and a clothes factory
readings.passageScript:
Look at the label inside your shirt. It says what the shirt is made of, and often where it was made. Behind those few words there is a long process.

Most shirts are made of cotton. Cotton is grown on farms in warm, dry places. The plant is watered for several months. Then the crop is harvested, by hand on small farms and by machine on large ones.

The cotton is taken to a mill, a building full of machines. There it is cleaned and processed. The short pieces are pulled into long threads. The threads are woven into fabric. Nothing here is done by one person. A crew of workers looks after a row of machines, and each machine does one job.

The fabric is sent to a factory. It is cut into pieces: two arms, a front and a back. The pieces are assembled at a long line of machines. Buttons are added last. Then the shirt is washed and packaged in a thin bag.

Now the shirt travels. Boxes are piled onto a lorry. Some shirts are sold in the same country. Many are exported, and arrive in a shop far away. In that shop they are imported goods.

Every step leaves waste: short pieces of cotton, fabric ends, water and thread. Some of the waste is used again. Some is thrown away. The profit on one shirt is small, so the industry makes very large numbers of them.

Read your label again. Cotton is a material. A shirt is a product. The two words are not the same, and the distance between them is this whole process.

readings.title: A work jacket label, and the notice at the gate
readings.setting: The label inside a jacket, and a board at a factory gate
readings.passageScript:
PRODUCT LABEL

Product: work jacket, dark blue.
Outer fabric: cotton. Buttons: steel. Lining: wool.
Assembled in workshop 4.
Packaged in paper, not in plastic.
Care: wash in cool water. Do not iron the badge.
Price: 45.
Repairs: free for one year. Bring this label with the jacket.

NOTICE AT THE FACTORY GATE

Opening times
The gate is open from 7 in the morning until 6 at night, Monday to Saturday.

Deliveries
Materials are delivered at the side gate only. Do not use the front gate.
Every delivery is checked before it is signed for.

Visitors
Report to the desk. A visitor card is given to you there.
Boots and a helmet are worn in the assembly hall. They are lent to you at the desk.

Repairs
Jackets under one year old are repaired free of charge.
Leave the jacket and the label at the desk. Repairs are finished in ten working days.
A message is sent to you when the work is done.

Waste
Fabric ends are collected on Thursday. Put them in the grey bin, not the black one.

Safety
Nothing above twenty kilos is lifted alone. Ask a member of the crew.

grammar.title: Is made, are grown, is sold
grammar.explanation: Often it does not matter who does the work. On a label you read: these boots are made of leather. Nobody is named, and nobody needs to be. English does this with two pieces: is or are, then the past form of the verb. The thing you are talking about goes to the front of the sentence.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
They make the bags here. The bags are made here.
They grow cotton on small farms. Cotton is grown on small farms.
They sell this bread in the market. This bread is sold in the market.
One thing: is made, is grown, is sold, is packaged.
More than one: are made, are grown, are sold, are packaged.
Ask about it: Where is it made? What is it made of?
Say no: The fabric is not imported.
Add by only when the doer matters: The boxes are packed by machine.
The past form is the same one you use after have: made, grown, sold, sent, built.
grammar.workedExample:
One done, step by step.
Item: Somebody grows the cotton on small farms.
Ask: does it matter who grows it? No.
So move the thing to the front: the cotton.
Cotton is one thing, so choose is.
The verb is grow. Its past form is grown.
Put the two pieces together: is grown.
Answer: Cotton is grown on small farms.
grammar.commonMistake: It is easy to stop after is or are: The bags are make here. English needs the past form as well. Write: The bags are made here. Say the two pieces together every time: are made.
grammar.memoryTip: Two pieces, never one: is or are, then made, grown, sold, sent. If you can say it after have, you can say it after is.
grammar.practice:
Write each sentence again, so that the thing comes first and nobody is named.
1. Somebody makes these boots in a small workshop.
2. They grow the fruit on farms up the valley.
3. Machines package the bread every morning.
4. Workers assemble the parts by hand.
5. They sell this product in every shop.
6. Somebody checks each jacket twice.
7. They do not import the wool.
8. Where do they manufacture the tools?
grammar.answerKey:
1. These boots are made in a small workshop. 2. The fruit is grown on farms up the valley. 3. The bread is packaged every morning by machine. 4. The parts are assembled by hand. 5. This product is sold in every shop. 6. Each jacket is checked twice. 7. The wool is not imported. 8. Where are the tools manufactured?
The likeliest wrong answer is 3: writing the bread is package. Package needs its past form, packaged.
Item 8 catches people the other way. The is or are comes before the thing in a question: Where are the tools manufactured?

grammar.title: Was delivered, were repaired
grammar.explanation: The same two pieces work for something that has already happened. Change is to was, and are to were. Nothing else moves, and the past form of the verb stays exactly the same: delivered, repaired, sold, made.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
The chair was repaired on Friday.
The boxes were delivered at the side gate.
The roof was built with steel and concrete.
The fabric was cut, and then it was packed.
One thing: was repaired, was sold, was sent.
More than one: were repaired, were sold, were sent.
Ask about it: When was it delivered? Where were they made?
Say no: The tools were not imported.
Now and then, side by side:
The bags are made here. The bags were made here last year.
grammar.workedExample:
One done, step by step.
Item: A crew repaired the roof last week.
Ask: does it matter who repaired it? Not here.
Move the thing to the front: the roof.
The roof is one thing, and this is the past, so choose was.
The verb is repair. Its past form is repaired.
Put the two pieces together: was repaired.
Answer: The roof was repaired last week.
grammar.commonMistake: It is easy to write the plain past on its own: The machine repaired on Tuesday. That says the machine did the repairing. Write: The machine was repaired on Tuesday.
grammar.memoryTip: Present takes is or are. Past takes was or were. The second piece never changes: repaired stays repaired.
grammar.practice:
Write each sentence again in the past, so that the thing comes first.
1. A crew delivered the materials on Monday.
2. Somebody repaired the two machines last month.
3. They packaged the jackets in paper.
4. A visitor lost the card.
5. They did not check the boxes.
6. When did they build the factory?
7. Somebody collected the waste on Thursday.
8. They exported most of the leather.
grammar.answerKey:
1. The materials were delivered on Monday. 2. The two machines were repaired last month. 3. The jackets were packaged in paper. 4. The card was lost. 5. The boxes were not checked. 6. When was the factory built? 7. The waste was collected on Thursday. 8. Most of the leather was exported.
The likeliest wrong answer is 2: writing the two machines was repaired. Two machines are more than one, so the word is were.
Item 6 is the other trap. The question word comes first, then was, then the thing: When was the factory built?

grammar.title: A crowd, a flock, a herd
grammar.explanation: One word can name a whole group. The group word is not free: each one goes with particular things. People stand in a crowd. Birds fly in a flock. Cows move in a herd. Choose the wrong one and the sentence sounds strange, even though every word in it is real.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
a crowd of people, a crowd of visitors
a flock of birds, a flock of sheep
a herd of cows, a herd of large animals
a bunch of keys, a bunch of bananas, a bunch of flowers
a set of tools, a set of plates
a pile of boxes, a pile of papers, a pile of waste
a crew of workers, a delivery crew
a collection of photos, a collection of old tools
The group word counts as one thing, so use is, was or has after it:
The crowd is large. The crew was small.
grammar.workedExample:
One done, step by step.
Item: Twenty birds sat on the factory roof.
Ask: what kind of thing are they? Birds.
Birds go with flock. A herd is for large animals only.
So the group is a flock of birds.
The group word counts as one thing, so use was and not were.
Answer: A flock of birds was sitting on the factory roof.
grammar.commonMistake: It is easy to put the wrong things together: a herd of birds. A herd is for large animals, such as cows. Birds go in a flock. Write: a flock of birds.
grammar.memoryTip: Learn the pair, not the word: crowd and people, flock and birds, herd and cows, bunch and keys, crew and workers.
grammar.practice:
Write the group word that fits.
1. A ____ of people waited outside the gate.
2. She carried a ____ of keys.
3. A ____ of six repaired the roof.
4. A ____ of birds crossed the field.
5. He keeps a ____ of old tools behind glass.
6. A ____ of boxes stood beside the door.
7. They bought a ____ of plates for the kitchen.
8. A ____ of cows blocked the road.
grammar.answerKey:
1. crowd 2. bunch 3. crew 4. flock 5. collection 6. pile 7. set 8. herd
The likeliest wrong answer is 8: writing flock. Cows are large animals, so they go in a herd. A flock is birds or sheep.
Item 5 catches people too. A collection is kept on purpose. A pile is only things put one on top of another.

grammar.title: Production, delivery, repair
grammar.explanation: A verb names the action: they produce, they deliver, they repair. A noun names the whole process: the production, the delivery, the repair. Labels and notices use the noun, because it is shorter. Four endings cover most of them, and a few words do not change at all.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
produce: the production
protect: the protection
collect: the collection
deliver: the delivery
assemble: the assembly
pay: the payment
agree: the agreement
package: the packaging
repair: the repair, with no change
waste: the waste, with no change
Use the noun after the, a or this, or after a describing word:
The delivery is on Friday. A free repair. This week's production.
grammar.workedExample:
One done, step by step.
Item: They deliver the boxes on Friday. Now turn deliver into a noun.
Ask: what is the verb? Deliver.
Deliver takes the ending -y: delivery.
Check the spelling letter by letter: d, e, l, i, v, e, r, y.
A noun follows the word the, so write it there.
Answer: The delivery is on Friday.
grammar.commonMistake: It is easy to leave the verb where a noun belongs: The deliver is on Friday. After the word the, English needs a noun. Write: The delivery is on Friday.
grammar.memoryTip: Say the pair out loud: produce, production. Deliver, delivery. Repair, repair. Your ear learns the ending faster than your eye.
grammar.practice:
Write the noun for each verb, then write it after the word the.
1. produce
2. deliver
3. collect
4. repair
5. protect
6. pay
7. assemble
8. package
grammar.answerKey:
1. production 2. delivery 3. collection 4. repair 5. protection 6. payment 7. assembly 8. packaging
Three of them end in -tion: production, collection and protection. Read those three out loud together.
The likeliest wrong answer is 4. Repair does not change at all, so the noun is the repair.
Item 7 is the other one to watch: assemble drops the -e and takes -y, giving assembly.

teacherNotes.reviewStatus: Reviewed: script review and curriculum sign-off, 2026-08-01
teacherNotes.note: The passive is two pieces, and learners drop the second one: the bags are make here. Do not explain it again. Have the learner say is made, are grown, was repaired out loud as pairs, ten times, before they write anything. The error is audible long before it is visible, and Speaking 1 exists for exactly that.

teacherNotes.reviewStatus: Reviewed: script review and curriculum sign-off, 2026-08-01
teacherNotes.note: The group words are not a list to memorise, they are pairs. A learner who studies crowd, flock, herd as eight separate words will still write a herd of birds. Ask them to say the pair every time: flock and birds, herd and cows, crew and workers. Practice 4 is built as pairs for that reason.

teacherNotes.reviewStatus: Reviewed: script review and curriculum sign-off, 2026-08-01
teacherNotes.note: Learners often add by somebody to every passive sentence, which undoes the point of the pattern. Keep by only when the doer is real information, as in the boxes are packed by machine. If the learner can delete by without losing anything, it should go.

teacherNotes.reviewStatus: Reviewed: script review and curriculum sign-off, 2026-08-01
teacherNotes.note: The endings are the hard part, not the meaning. Three of the eight in Practice 5 take -tion, one takes -ment, two take -y, and one does not change at all. Have the learner sort the eight nouns into those four piles before they try to spell them from memory.

teacherNotes.reviewStatus: Reviewed: script review and curriculum sign-off, 2026-08-01
teacherNotes.note: The tutor is a rehearsal partner here, not a marking service. It is useful for taking the question side of Speaking 5, for naming a group of things and letting the learner supply the group word, and for reading the gate notice aloud at different speeds. Every task in this unit carries its own answer key, so nothing depends on the tutor's opinion.
